name: AINews
why: Every issue's recap has a cluster of evals, often under a New evals heading. Good for launches that never become papers, such as BallotBench and Immigration Bench.

name: Don't Worry About the Vase
why: The weekly AI roundup has an On Your Marks section on benchmarks and evals, with Zvi's take on what they show.

name: Import AI
why: Half of recent issues lead with a named benchmark, most of them new, and Clark says why he thinks it matters.

name: The Epoch Brief
cadence: One or two posts a week
why: Announces Epoch's own new benchmarks and its Benchmark Reviews.

name: Interconnects
cadence: One to three posts a week
why: Mostly about open models and post-training, with the occasional long post on a new eval.

name: SemiAnalysis
by: Dylan Patel and the SemiAnalysis team
why: Launches its own benchmarks in the newsletter, such as GDPx in November 2026. Most posts are about chips and datacenters, so we take only launches.

name: Dwarkesh Podcast
why: Launched Clocktower Bench in a post and video essay in November 2026. Most posts are podcast episodes, so we take only launches.

name: Prime Intellect blog
why: Publishes audits of public evaluations, such as its November 2026 review of AutomationBench, OfficeQA Pro v2 and HLE-Diamond. We read it for the audit queue on the New page.

name: Bluesky
by: Labs, evaluators and the tech press
why: Labs and evaluators often post their X launch threads here too, and Techmeme posts its headlines. We search for launch wording such as “releasing” or “new benchmark”.

name: Daily Papers
why: About one paper in five is a new benchmark. Each comes with upvotes, the authors' organization and a code link, so they're easy to rank.

name: arXiv
why: No other feed catches as many new benchmarks. But the bulk of hits only mention a benchmark, so we filter hard.

name: NeurIPS Evaluations and Datasets track
why: Every accepted paper is a peer-reviewed dataset or evaluation. They arrive in one batch each fall.
manual: OpenReview's API now needs a signed-in account to list papers. We'll read this track automatically once we have one.

name: Benchmarking Hub
why: A curated list with independent runs and a capability index. A new row in its metadata means a benchmark worth tracking. Our independent runs come from here.

name: Inspect Evals
why: Each new eval gets its own folder, so a new folder means someone has packaged a benchmark to run.

name: Harbor Hub
why: Labs and vendors publish agent task sets here first, ready to run. Some entries are only tests, so finds from here need a closer look.

name: Environments Hub
why: New eval and training environments every day. Most are for reinforcement learning, and only a few are benchmarks.

name: Every Eval Ever
why: A shared store of results on thousands of benchmarks. A new collection folder means a new benchmark has been added.

name: Official benchmark datasets
why: Hugging Face's own allow-list of evaluation datasets that model cards can report results on. Every entry is a real benchmark.

name: Benchmark datasets with results
why: New datasets tagged benchmark whose card reports results for at least three current models from two or more labs, such as ShadowBench. About 60 datasets a day get the tag and most have no results. This finds about two a day, from lab releases to personal projects, so its finds wait on the watch list until a second source names them.

name: VLMEvalKit
why: New multimodal and video benchmarks land here within weeks of their papers.

name: Vals AI
why: Vals builds its own benchmarks for law, finance, medicine and tax, and announces each one on its blog.

name: SEAL leaderboards
why: Scale publishes its own new benchmarks here, each with a dated post.
manual: New Scale boards are added by hand. Once added, each board's scores are read from its public page (scripts/lib/scale.ts).

name: Artificial Analysis
cadence: New evaluations several times a month
why: Its changelog announces each evaluation it adopts.
manual: We are currently unable to feature AA benchmarks due to their terms of service.

name: Arena
why: Adds new arenas a few times a year. We read its published dataset instead of the site.

name: Lab model cards and system cards
by: Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Ai2, Qwen, DeepSeek, Moonshot and others
why: Labs with closed models publish results in launch posts and system cards. Open-weight labs put their tables in Hugging Face READMEs.
manual: We read launch posts from Google DeepMind, Google, Mistral and Ai2 automatically, along with new open-weight model cards on Hugging Face. Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, DeepSeek and Kimi bar automated reading of their own sites, so we check those by hand.

name: awesome-ai-leaderboard
why: The most active general list of AI leaderboards.

name: Awesome-CUA
why: Structured, dated records of computer-use agent benchmarks, kept current by a scanner.

name: BenchmarkList
why: A large catalog of about 2,600 benchmarks, including vendor and independent boards that have no paper, such as LifeSci Diamond. We read its public data API once a day for reference: new entries' names and their own links, which we check at the source. We copy none of its text or scores.

name: Benchmark launches on X
by: Researchers and labs, searched by Grok
why: Most launches that are not papers start as an X thread, such as ShadowBench and DeepFinance. We never fetch X. Grok Build, xAI's command-line agent, searches X with its own tools, and we check every link it returns at the source.
feed: Grok Build (grok -p) with its X search, on a maintainer's computer
